title: Hosts and guests
cando: offer, invite, give instructions and check what someone means

about.text: In this lesson you are a host, and a guest comes to your flat. You invite people, offer drinks and snacks, and explain how something works. You also check what people mean, and you write an invitation and two replies.
goals: Welcome a guest and offer something: Would you like a coffee?
Invite someone: Would you like to come for dinner on Friday?
Give instructions in order: Press it, then pull it. Don't push it.
Check what someone means: Sorry, which one do you mean?
Write an invitation, and a reply to say yes or no.

chapters.title: A guest at the door
chapters.text:
In this lesson you are the host. A guest comes to your home.
First, you listen to Mei. Her new neighbour, Kwame, comes for a drink on Saturday.
Mei says: Come in! Would you like a cold drink, or a coffee?
Kwame says: It's warm today, isn't it? The short question at the end is a tag.
Kwame is sure. He only wants Mei to agree. So his voice goes down on the tag. Listen for it.
Then Mei explains how the front door of the building works.

chapters.title: Offers, invitations and instructions
chapters.text:
There are two grammar points in this lesson.
One. To offer a thing, say: Would you like a coffee? Would you like a biscuit?
To invite someone, add to and a verb: Would you like to come for dinner?
Two. Instructions start with a verb: Press the button. Twist the key.
To say what not to do, use don't: Don't push the door. Pull it.
Put the steps in order: first, then, after that, finally.

chapters.title: Tea for a guest
chapters.text:
Next, you read a notice in an office kitchen. Its title is: How to make tea for a guest.
It has six steps. Most steps say what to do. Some say what not to do: Don't fill the kettle to the top.
Read it slowly. The order of the steps is important.
Then you write an invitation, and two replies. One reply says yes, and one says no.
A polite no often starts with unfortunately.

chapters.title: Be the host
chapters.text:
In the task, you are the host. A new colleague comes to your home for a coffee.
Welcome him, and offer drinks. Then explain how your coffee machine works, step by step.
At the end, check that he understood. Ask: Is that clear? Or ask him to say the steps back to you.
Then invite him to something else.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a story or an article about hosts and guests.
Read it once for the main idea. Then read it again and answer the questions.

warmup.prompt: A guest arrives at your home. What do you say first?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people say two of these together: Hi! Come in! Then they offer a drink.

conversation.title: A guest at the door
conversation.setting: It is Saturday afternoon. Kwame moved into the flat upstairs last week. His neighbour Mei invited him for a drink. He knocks on her door.
lines: Hi, Kwame! Come in, come in.
Hello, Mei. Thanks for inviting me. It's warm today, isn't it?
It is! Would you like a cold drink, or a coffee?
Here you are. And would you like a biscuit? They're lovely.
Yes, please. Your flat is very tidy!
Thanks! So, how's your new flat? Is everything OK?
It's great. But the front door of the building is strange. I can't open it from the inside.
Oh, it's easy. Press the white button, then pull the door. Don't push it.
Sorry, which button do you mean? The big one?
No, the small white one, next to the door. And at night, lock it. Twist the key two times.
Press the button, then pull. At night, twist the key two times. That's clear. Thanks!
You're welcome. Would you like to come for dinner on Friday? My sister is a great cook.
I'd love to, thank you. You like cooking too, don't you?

questions.q: What does Kwame want to drink?
questions.why: Kwame says: Just some water, please.

questions.q: How do you open the front door from the inside?
questions.a: Press the white button, then pull the door.
questions.why: Mei says: Press the white button, then pull the door. Don't push it.

questions.q: What does Mei invite Kwame to?
questions.why: Mei says: Would you like to come for dinner on Friday?

phrases.use: Asking a guest to come into your home.
What a guest often says when they arrive.

phrases.text: Would you like to come for dinner?

items.meaning: The person who invites guests and looks after them.
items.example: Mei is a great host. Her guests always feel welcome.

items.meaning: A person you invite to your home, or to a party or a meal.
items.example: We've got two guests for dinner on Saturday.

items.meaning: To ask someone if they would like something.
items.example: The receptionist offered me a coffee.

items.meaning: To ask someone to come to your home, a meal or a party.
items.example: I invited my new neighbour for a drink.

items.meaning: A small, flat, sweet thing to eat, often with tea or coffee.
items.example: Would you like a biscuit with your tea?

items.meaning: A little food that you eat between meals.
items.example: I have a snack at eleven o'clock, usually some fruit.

items.meaning: Very nice, or very beautiful. People in Britain say it a lot.
items.example: Thank you for a lovely evening.

items.meaning: With everything in the right place.
items.example: Your kitchen is always so tidy!

items.meaning: To push something with your finger.
items.example: Press the green button to start.

items.meaning: To turn something with your hand, like a key or the top of a bottle.
items.example: Twist the key two times to lock the door.

items.meaning: To close a door with a key, so nobody can open it.
items.example: Please lock the door when you leave.

items.meaning: What a word or a sentence says. Also, what someone wants to say.
items.example: What's the meaning of this word?

items.meaning: Easy to understand, or easy to see.
items.example: Your instructions are very clear. Thank you.

items.meaning: Very sure. You know that something is true.
items.example: Are you certain the shop opens at nine?

sound.title: The tag on the end
sound.explain: A tag is the short question at the end: isn't it? don't you? A sentence with not takes a tag with no not: It isn't far, is it? When you are sure, your voice goes down on the tag. When you are not sure, it goes up. Listen, then say each group.
groups: It's warm, isn't it? · It's lovely, isn't it?
You like cooking, don't you? · You work here, don't you?
It isn't far, is it? · You don't drive, do you?
lines: You like cooking too, don't you?
The key is in the door, isn't it?

sayIt.instructions: Say Kwame's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Does your voice go down on isn't it and don't you?
lines: Hello, Mei. Thanks for inviting me. It's warm today, isn't it?
Yes, please. Your flat is very tidy!
Sorry, which button do you mean? The big one?
I'd love to, thank you. You like cooking too, don't you?

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from the conversation. Two offer or invite. Three tell Kwame what to do.
examples: Would you like a cold drink, or a coffee?
Would you like to come for dinner on Friday?
Press the white button, then pull the door.
spot.question: Which sentence offers a thing, and which invites Kwame to do something? What comes after to? How do the instructions start?
spot.answer: Would you like + a thing offers: a cold drink. Would you like to + a verb invites: to come. The instructions start with a verb: press, pull, twist. Don't + a verb says what not to do: Don't push it.

rules.title: Would you like a …? Would you like to …?
rule: Offer a thing: Would you like a coffee? Would you like some water?
Invite someone: Would you like to come for dinner? Would you like to sit down?
Say yes: Yes, please. I'd love to. Say no: No, thank you. I'm fine.
Would you like …? is more polite than Do you want …?
Ask for yourself with I'd like: I'd like a glass of water, please.
rules.mistake: Not: Would you like come for dinner? Say: Would you like to come for dinner?

rules.title: Instructions in order: press it, then don't pull it
rule: Start with the verb: Press the button. Twist the key.
Say it or them after the verb: Press it. Lock it. Wash them.
Say what not to do with don't: Don't push it. Don't open it.
Give a reason after don't: Don't open it. It's very hot.
Put the steps in order: First, … Then … After that, … Finally, …
rules.mistake: Not: No push the door. Not: Don't to push it. Say: Don't push the door.

practice.why: Would you like + a thing: a biscuit.

practice.q: Would you like ___ for dinner on Saturday?
practice.why: Would you like to + a verb invites someone.
The short, polite answer is: Yes, please.
Don't + a verb says what not to do.

practice.q: The kettle is hot. Don't ___ it.
practice.why: Don't + a verb, with no to and no -ing.

practice.q: This is the button. Press ___ , then wait.
These are the cups. Please wash ___ after the meeting.
practice.why: More than one cup: wash them.

practice.q: First, fill the kettle. Then press the switch. ___ , pour the water into the mug.
practice.why: Finally is for the last step.

practice.q: ___ like to sit down? You look tired.
practice.why: Would you like to …? is a polite invitation.

yourTurn.prompt: A colleague visits your home for the first time. Write what you say. Welcome them, offer two things, and explain how one thing in your home works.
yourTurn.model: Come in, Priya! Would you like a cup of tea or some juice? Would you like to sit by the window? It's nice and warm there. The window is a bit strange. First, twist the handle. Then push it. Don't pull it hard. It's very old.

text.title: How to make tea for a guest
text.body:
PRACTICE NOTICE: for English practice only.

KITCHEN, THIRD FLOOR
HOW TO MAKE TEA FOR A GUEST
Have you got a visitor? Please offer them a hot drink. Read all the steps first.

1. Fill the kettle with cold water. Don't fill it to the top.
2. Press the switch at the back. Wait about two minutes.
3. Don't open the kettle. It is very hot.
4. Put one tea bag in each mug. Then pour in the hot water slowly.
5. Wait three minutes. Then take the tea bags out.
6. Ask your guest: Would you like milk? Would you like sugar?

Milk is in the fridge. Put some in a small jug.
Biscuits are in the blue tin, next to the trays.
Put the mugs, the jug and the biscuits on a tray, with two napkins.
Carry the tray slowly, with two hands.

After your guest leaves, please wash everything and put it back.
Thank you!
The Office Manager

gist.a: It tells staff how to make tea for a visitor.
wrong: It invites staff to a party.
It asks staff to buy a new kettle.
gist.why: The title is: How to make tea for a guest.
It says: Kitchen, third floor. It is from the office manager.

detail.q: How long does the kettle take?
detail.why: Step 2 says: Wait about two minutes.

detail.q: Why don't you open the kettle?
detail.why: Step 3 says: Don't open the kettle. It is very hot.

detail.q: When do you take the tea bags out?
detail.why: Step 5 says: Wait three minutes. Then take the tea bags out.

detail.a: in the blue tin, next to the trays
wrong: in the fridge, next to the milk
in the cupboard, next to the mugs
detail.why: The notice says: Biscuits are in the blue tin, next to the trays.

items.meaning: A machine that boils water, for tea or coffee.
items.example: Can you fill the kettle, please?

items.meaning: A big cup with a handle, for hot drinks.
items.example: I drink my coffee from a big blue mug.

items.meaning: A small or tall pot with a handle. You pour milk or water from it.
items.example: There's a jug of water on the table.

items.meaning: A flat board for carrying cups, plates and food.
items.example: She brought the drinks in on a tray.

items.meaning: A piece of paper or cloth. You clean your hands and mouth with it when you eat.
items.example: Put a napkin next to each plate.

items.meaning: A small paper packet of dry leaves. Put it in hot water, and you have a hot drink.
items.example: Put one tea bag in each mug.

items.meaning: When you ask someone to come to a party, a meal or your home. It can be a card or a message.
items.example: Thanks for the invitation! I'd love to come.

items.meaning: To say yes to an offer or an invitation.
items.example: Kwame accepted the invitation to dinner.

items.meaning: To say no to an offer or an invitation.
items.example: I had to refuse, because I was working that day.

items.meaning: To answer a message, an email or a letter.
items.example: Please reply by Friday.

items.meaning: A polite word before bad news. It means: I'm sorry, but …
items.example: Unfortunately, I can't come on Saturday.

model.title: An invitation, a yes and a no
model.body:
1. THE INVITATION
Hi Tomasz,
Would you like to come for lunch at my flat on Sunday? Come at one o'clock. There's soup and fresh bread. My address is Flat 3, 14 Park Road. Please reply by Friday.
Mei
2. A YES
Hi Mei,
Thank you for the invitation! I'd love to come. Can I bring anything?
Tomasz
3. A NO
Hi Mei,
Thank you for the invitation. Unfortunately, I can't come on Sunday. I have to work all day. Would you like to meet for coffee next week?
Omar

write.task: Write an invitation to a colleague or a friend: for lunch, dinner or a coffee. Say the day, the time and the place. Then write two short replies: one to say yes, and one to say no.
checklist: My invitation has Would you like to …? and a day, a time and a place.
My yes says thank you and I'd love to come.
My no says thank you, unfortunately, and a reason.
I wrote a name at the end of each message.

card.title: Be the host
card.situation: Your new colleague Carlos comes to your flat on Saturday for a coffee. It's his first visit. Your coffee machine is a bit strange, and he wants to make a second coffee himself.
card.goal: Welcome Carlos and offer him two drinks. Explain how the coffee machine works, in order. Check he understood. Then invite him to something else.

phrases: Come in! Would you like a tea or a coffee?
First, put a mug under it. Then press the big button.
Don't press it again. Wait for the green light.
Is that clear? What do you do first?
Would you like to come for lunch next week?
prepare.notes: Write your steps for the coffee machine, or for another thing in your home. Write four steps, in order. One step starts with Don't.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, your teacher is Carlos. Welcome him and offer drinks. Explain how your coffee machine works, then check he understood. Then change roles.
doIt.wehel: You are my new colleague Carlos. You come to my flat for a coffee. I welcome you and offer you drinks. Then I explain how my coffee machine works. Ask me one question to check what I mean. Then say the steps back to me. Use simple English.

model.title: Coffee at home
lines: Hi Carlos, come in! It's cold today, isn't it?
It is! Thanks for inviting me.
Would you like a tea or a coffee?
A coffee, please. With milk, but no sugar.
OK. This coffee machine is a bit strange. First, put the mug under it.
Then press the big button once. Don't press it again. Just wait for the green light.
Sorry, what do you mean by the green light?
This small light here. When it's green, the coffee is ready. Is that clear?
Yes. The mug under it, press the button once, and wait for the green light.
Perfect! Would you like a biscuit with it?
And would you like to come for lunch next Saturday? My brother is a great cook.
compare: Did you welcome your guest and offer a drink with Would you like …?
Did you give the steps in order, with one Don't?
Did you check: Is that clear? Did your guest say the steps back?
Did you invite your guest with Would you like to …?

canDo: I can welcome a guest and offer food and drinks.
I can invite someone with Would you like to …?
I can explain how something works, step by step.
I can check what someone means, and check that they understood me.
I can write an invitation, and a reply to say yes or no.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first picture. Who is the host? Who is the guest? What do you think happens?
reading.talk: Was the host in the story a good host? What do you offer a guest in your home? Write three sentences, or say them to Wehel.

quiz.why: Would you like to + a verb invites someone.
A polite no: No, thank you.
Don't + a verb, with no to.
It's cold has no not, so the tag has not: isn't it?
A kettle is a machine that boils water.

quiz.q: A friend invites you to dinner, but you are busy. How do you start your reply?
quiz.why: Unfortunately comes before bad news, like a no.

quiz.q: You don't understand an instruction. What do you say?
quiz.why: This asks the person to explain again.

quiz.q: Mei ___ start work at eight. It's a rule.
quiz.why: Mei is she, so has to. A rule means there is no choice.

quiz.q: Sorry, I'm busy. I ___ a report for my manager.
She works 20 hours a week, so her job is ___ .
quiz.why: Only some hours of the week: part-time.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the guest at the door conversation in pairs. Then change the drinks and the snacks. Practise the tags: the voice goes down when you are sure.
Day 2: an offer circle. Each learner offers something with Would you like …?, and the next learner accepts or refuses. Then each learner gives three instructions for a phone, a door or a machine.
Day 3: the task. You are the guest. Each learner welcomes you, offers drinks, explains their coffee machine and checks you understood.
Day 4: talk about the book, answer questions, and read two invitations and their replies aloud.
